Oscar's Final Fight

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Canoeing legend Oscar Chalupsky has survived the toughest oceans in the world. Now he's fighting terminal cancer, and a medical aid system he says would rather fund lawyers than life-saving treatment.

Unique Selling Point:
Oscar Chalupsky’s fight against cancer has exposed a high-stakes legal battle over whether medical aids must pay for modern, life-saving treatments.

Summary:
Oscar Chalupsky is a 62-year-old canoeing legend now fighting for his life. The renowned South African paddler captained the national team at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics and is a 12-time World Surfski Champion. In 2019, he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that affects plasma cells. While once considered a death sentence, major medical advances in recent years have transformed how the disease can be treated.

Chalupsky began treatment in 2020. In 2023, after his maintenance therapy failed, his oncologist prescribed Daratumumab or Darzalex, a targeted cancer drug now widely used internationally. Despite multiple myeloma being classified as a prescribed minimum benefit under the Medical Schemes Act, which legally requires medical aids to fund treatment regardless of plan type, Discovery Health Medical Scheme agreed to cover only 50 percent of the cost.

As a result, Chalupsky was left to pay about R275,000 out of pocket. He lodged a formal complaint with the Council for Medical Schemes, where his legal team argued the treatment was clinically justified and should have been funded in full. Discovery, however, argued the medication fell outside its approved sequencing for this cancer. The Council ruled in Chalupsky’s favour. Discovery refused to pay and has since appealed the decision twice. Discovery's appeal was due to be heard in March, but in an about turn the medical scheme withdrew the appeal just days before our scheduled interview with the CEO. The last ruling was delivered in April 2025, yet the appeal was withdrawn eight months later. Why the delay? Oscar went public with his fight with Discovery in December, and the response was overwhelming.

Chalupsky has chosen to make his battle public, saying he is fighting not only for himself but for hundreds of patients facing similar denials. He told me a priest has read him his last rites twice in the past two years, yet he refuses to give up. Discovery has spent an estimated six million rand on legal costs, instead of reimbursing the R275,000. Chalupsky says the scheme, which reports billions in annual profit and has millions of members, is prioritising shareholders over patients.

He has received free legal representation and says he has been overwhelmed by public support. A post detailing his struggle on social media drew more than 500,000 engagements. Chalupsky also established a personal fund called No Retreat, No Surrender, which enabled him to seek treatment in China. Within two weeks, he raised two million rand. That treatment ended due to unforeseen circumstances, and he is now preparing to participate in a clinical trial in the United States.

Lauren Pretorius from Campaigning for Cancer says South Africa’s medical funding models urgently need reform. She has spent years advocating for cancer patients and says treatments that were unavailable a decade ago are now standard elsewhere, yet often inaccessible locally. Doctors, she says, are forced to rely on outdated therapies because medical aids refuse to fund innovation. She believes patients deserve transparency about what their monthly contributions truly cover.

Meanwhile, Chalupsky continues to train three times a day, even while on chemotherapy and steroids. He says he feels a responsibility to fight for those who do not have the same support. “Most people lose the will to fight,” he says. “I won’t.”

Script:


VO 1 Big swells in False Bay and strong winds - challenging conditions that test the strongest athletes.

NATSOUND Subtitles: It’s blowing between 40 and 80 km/h winds. What we’re going to try and do today is go through the lighthouse.

VO 2 For surfski multiple world champion Oscar Chalupsky, this is where he feels most alive.

VO 3 The 62 year old has spent most of his life winning endurance competitions at the highest level.

VO 4 But, he’s had to take on a new challenge - fighting for his medical aid rights in a life or death struggle against cancer.

NATSOUND Subtitles: That was proper.

FADE TO BLACK

VO 5 We meet Oscar on a perfect summer's day in Cape Town, to head out on calm seas.

NATSOUND Oscar: Cape Town’s performing. Erin: Gorgeous

VO 6 Dave, the owner of this yacht, and friends with Oscar for decades, creates a wake giving Oscar the chance to train.

VO 7 For his wife, Clare, getting Oscar to slow down, has never been easy.

NATSOUND Clare Chalupsky: Oscar don’t overdo it!

NATSOUND: Oscar: And we’re out. Erin: There you go. Oscar: Well done.

UPSOUND Oscar Chalupsky: Since I was six years old, I spent all my time in the ocean. To me, this is sort of a cleansing. People meditate. I get in the ocean and I can paddle for 80kms because I just love it.

VO 8 Oscar’s father was a top paddler and introduced him to the sport when he was about ten years old. His athletic ability was clear from a young age.

UPSOUND Oscar Chalupsky: And the reason why I was doing so well is I was twice the size of everybody else, so you had no chance you know because I was much bigger. I had like a growth spurt.

VO 9 In the world of surfsking, he’s known as the “Big O” His sporting achievements are legendary. And include winning the Molokai surfski challenge twelve times. It’s regarded as one of the world’s most gruelling ocean races.

NATSOUND Oscar Chalupsky from South Africa.

VO 10 When he began experiencing back pain in 2019, he initially dismissed it.

NATSOUND Oscar: We used to have a race that finished in here. It went from Houtbay, finished inside here.

VO 11 The pain was being caused by a tumour on his spine and he was told he had multiple myeloma - an incurable cancer of plasma cells that live in the bone marrow.

UPSOUND Oscar Chalupsky: You know, you never think its going to happen to you. You think you’re bullet proof. Especially especially me. I was like, I was in pain but because I’m a sportsman I never even worried about the pain. This just goes with the territory.

VO 12 Oscar and Clare were living in Portugal at the time, and he was initially given less than six months to live.

UPSOUND Oscar Chalupsky: My bloods were so bad, I couldn’t’ even fly. My first goal was to get on an aeroplane. I didn’t want to have the funeral in Portugal, I’d rather have it in South Africa. So my first goal was just to get on that plane and I did.

VO 13 Six years later, he continues to defy the odds.

ERIN: How does fighting cancer compare with your toughest race?

UPSOUND Oscar Chalupsky: I think they’re basically exactly the same. I mean the bottom line is when I think about that race in 2012 at the age of 49 winning my 12th Molokai, I pushed my body to the nth degree, and it’s basically all in your mind. And I think that’s the most important thing. If you’ve got a positive attitude to fight anything, you can overcome everything, but you have to have the positive attitude.

VO 14 Oscar has received numerous treatments. Multiple myeloma goes through cycles where the cancer is brought under control, known as remission, before it returns - attacking the body more aggressively each time.

UPSOUND Oscar Chalupsky: When I first got diagnosed, I had a stem cell transplant, so basically die and come back again, basically a new lease of life, and then that stopped working, and then I went onto this drug which was going very well. And then they said no, Discovery said no we’re not going to pay for this.

VO 15 Oscar has been a member of Discovery Health Medical Scheme, South Africa’s largest medical aid company, for years and when it refused to pay the full costs for a drug called Darzalex, he didn’t question it. He paid for co-payments from his own pocket.

UPSOUND Oscar Chalupsky: So, I just kept on paying myself only to find out later that Campaigning for Cancer, an ngo said no no no they should have been paying. And that’s how it all started. And I think a lot of people out there don’t even know their rights.

VO 16 Campaigning for Cancer helped him lodge a complaint with the Council for Medical Schemes or CMS in January 2024.

VO 17 The CMS ruled that Discovery should have paid for 100 percent of the drug. And ordered the scheme to pay up.

UPSOUND Oscar Chalupsky: I’ve been paying for thirty years to Discovery, and I’m one of those healthiest people, that never ever used my money, never claimed. I never was in hospital, and then suddenly this happens.

VO 18 But Discovery dug in its heels, refusing to pay more than it had already paid - and appealed. A second time, the CMS found in Oscar’s favour. Again, Discovery appealed, seeking a third ruling.

VO 19 Frustrated by the lengthy process, Oscar took his fight public on social media in December last year.

VO 20 He was overwhelmed by the response.

UPSOUND Oscar Chalupsky: You don’t realise until you do and say something how, what an impact. I mean I saw there was 500 000 likes and comments so that you really realise my gosh this is bigger than me.

UPSOUND Clare Chalupsky: People who are ill you know they are are always told to try and manage their stress.

VO 21 Oscar’s wife Clare has supported him in his fight against Discovery Health, not just for him, but for the thousands of others facing similar battles..

UPSOUND Clare Chalupsky: When you have monetary problems or issues it really compounds the patient and and the family.

VO 22 Oscar’s haemotologist Dr Perry Loebenberg says its becoming increasingly common, particularly with cancer therapies, for medical aid schemes to only partially cover treatment.

UPSOUND Dr Perry Loebenberg / Haemotologist: Discovery ultimately don’t decide what the correct treatment is for you. But they decide what they’ll pay for or not in accordance with their rules. These patients are already under a great amount of stress. To be told that there’s more effective treatment that can prolong your life by a significant amount if we can include it only to be effectively declined that treatment on financial grounds, I think really robs people of their spirit to fight and to continue to battle against the cancer.

VO 23 It’s been two years since Oscar challenged Discovery’s decision not to pay for the drug he needed in full - but if anyone could survive the lengthy process it was Oscar.

LINK: Oscar’s case shows that medical aid members have power. Where medical aid schemes decline the payment of treatment, those rulings can be challenged.

VO 24 Discovery Health’s CEO Dr Ron Whelan says the scheme has paid over R3 million for Oscar’s treatments since diagnosis - including about a million rand for Darzalex.

VO 25 And, in the same interview, he shared some breaking - some might say, surprising - news.

UPSOUND Dr Ron Whelan / Discovery Health CEO: And in fact Erin, I’m pleased to let you know that the latest available evidence that got presented in early January this year you know confirmed that the second line treatment was probably not appropriate for Oscar’s treatment at the time. And on the basis of that information, the scheme decided to withdraw the appeal, so the appeal was withdrawn in late January now this year. As evidence evolves and as data evolves and new evidence comes to light, it’s our obligation to change our view if the evidence supports the patient. I think what is important in this particular matter is it’s not about the money.

ERIN: Come now! It’s all about the money. That’s the whole nub of the issue, is getting the money you need, to get the medication you require to fight the condition.

UPSOUND Dr Ron Whelan: It’s about ensuring that we can provide sustainable access to medications for both the individual and the collective.

VO 26 Discovery will have to pay IN FULL for his darzalex going forward. But, Oscar says he’s still owed over R250 000 for the co payments he made. Discovery says the amount is far less.

UPSOUND Dr Ron Whelan: 95 percent of the cost of Oscar’s darzalex treatment was already funded by the medical scheme together with a pharmaceutical company through a co pay support programme. There was an outstanding amount of I think R37,000. Which..

ERIN: Which you didn’t want to pay.

UPSOUND Ron Whelan: Well importantly, our interest is the individual as well as the collective. If I make an exception for Oscar, we got to be willing to make an exception for everyone across the medical scheme.

VO 27 While lawyers haggle over the settlement, Oscar’s victory may set a precedent for others in his position.

VO 28 He’s physically fit and still trains every day.

UPSOUND Clare Chalupsky: Our children even say we don’t think of dad as being sick. He’s just out there just doing what he’s always done and what he’s always loved to do. So, he uplifts us, as hopefully we give him strength.

VO 29 For Oscar, giving up has never been an option.

VO 30 He’s been accepted onto a clinical trial in the United States, with plans to travel there in April.

UPSOUND Oscar Chalupsky: So, my last roll of my dice. It might buy me one to three years depends how it works. You know, at the moment they’ve got no cure but I think in 2 or 3 years with AI they might find a cure, and I might be here longer than you think.

The renowned South African paddler captained the national team at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics and is a 12-time World Surfski Champion. In 2019, he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that affects plasma cells. While once considered a death sentence, major medical advances in recent years have transformed how the disease can be treated. Chalupsky began treatment in 2020. In 2023, after his maintenance therapy failed, his oncologist prescribed Daratumumab or Darzalex, a targeted cancer drug now widely used internationally. Despite multiple myeloma being classified as a prescribed minimum benefit under the Medical Schemes Act, which legally requires medical aids to fund treatment regardless of plan type, Discovery Health Medical Scheme agreed to cover only 50 percent of the cost. As a result, Chalupsky was left to pay about R275,000 out of pocket. He lodged a formal complaint with the Council for Medical Schemes, where his legal team argued the treatment was clinically justified and should have been funded in full. Discovery, however, argued the medication fell outside its approved sequencing for this cancer. The Council ruled in Chalupsky’s favour. Discovery refused to pay and has since appealed the decision twice. Discovery's appeal was due to be heard in March, but in an about turn the medical scheme withdrew the appeal just days before our scheduled interview with the CEO. The last ruling was delivered in April 2025, yet the appeal was withdrawn eight months later. Why the delay? Oscar went public with his fight with Discovery in December, and the response was overwhelming. Chalupsky has chosen to make his battle public, saying he is fighting not only for himself but for hundreds of patients facing similar denials. He told me a priest has read him his last rites twice in the past two years, yet he refuses to give up. Discovery has spent an estimated six million rand on legal costs, instead of reimbursing the R275,000. Chalupsky says the scheme, which reports billions in annual profit and has millions of members, is prioritising shareholders over patients. He has received free legal representation and says he has been overwhelmed by public support. A post detailing his struggle on social media drew more than 500,000 engagements. Chalupsky also established a personal fund called No Retreat, No Surrender, which enabled him to seek treatment in China. Within two weeks, he raised two million rand. That treatment ended due to unforeseen circumstances, and he is now preparing to participate in a clinical trial in the United States. Lauren Pretorius from Campaigning for Cancer says South Africa’s medical funding models urgently need reform. She has spent years advocating for cancer patients and says treatments that were unavailable a decade ago are now standard elsewhere, yet often inaccessible locally. Doctors, she says, are forced to rely on outdated therapies because medical aids refuse to fund innovation. She believes patients deserve transparency about what their monthly contributions truly cover. Meanwhile, Chalupsky continues to train three times a day, even while on chemotherapy and steroids. He says he feels a responsibility to fight for those who do not have the same support. “Most people lose the will to fight,” he says. “I won’t.”
